message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for me to say "See you next year!" to this teacher who's getting let go. Let me start by understanding the situation better. First, this teacher, let's call him Mr. R, was new at my school this year. From the start, he tried to impose his own way of teaching and grading, which was very different from what we, the students, had ever experienced. It seems like he expected us to do things his way, even if his methods were wrong and people pointed that out to him. That sounds pretty rigid and not open to feedback. Mr. R also took off points for scratch work that he didn't like and tried to take off as many points as possible on tests, quizzes, and homework. Every student he had was subjected to this, without exception. That sounds really harsh and unfair. It's one thing to have strict grading, but when it's consistently harsh and not based on clear criteria, it can be demoralizing for students. Additionally, Mr. R took forever to grade our assignments. We took a test the week before spring break and got it back about six weeks later. That's a long time, and it probably made it hard for us to learn from our mistakes since the material was already covered. He also refused to go over the test with anyone, which is another missed opportunity for us to understand where we went wrong and how to improve. Mr. R never offered help outside of the classroom and was hostile whenever asked for extra help. That's really unfortunate because students often need additional support, and a teacher who isn't willing to provide that is not being very helpful. The administration noticed these issues, and we were informed that Mr. R wasn't coming back next year. It's no surprise that we were overjoyed about this news. After the announcement, Mr. R completely checked out. He wrote notes on the board, barely talked during class, and even went to Disneyland instead of attending one of the review days for exams. That seems like a lack of responsibility and commitment to his students. Yesterday, as I was walking out of Mr. R's classroom for the last time, I called out, "See you next year!" over my shoulder. My friends told me I'm the asshole for this, but I don't think so. I'm trying to figure out if I was right or wrong to say that. So, why did I say that? Maybe I was trying to get a reaction or make a point. But considering how Mr. R treated us and how he checked out after the announcement, maybe I felt justified in saying something like that. However, my friends think it's wrong, so I need to consider their perspective as well. Is it wrong to say something like that to a teacher who's being let go? On one hand, Mr. R wasn't a good teacher, and his behavior was harmful to the students. On the other hand, saying "See you next year!" might come off as disrespectful or mocking, especially since he wasn't coming back. I also need to think about the impact of my words. Did it make the situation worse? Did it affect how others saw me or how I was perceived by the teacher or the administration? It's possible that it could have been seen as unprofessional or mean-spirited, especially if the teacher was already struggling or feeling down about being let go. But then again, I was just expressing my feelings about the situation. I was happy that Mr. R wasn't coming back because he wasn't a good teacher, and I wanted to make sure he knew how we felt. However, there are more constructive ways to express that sentiment without being disrespectful. Maybe I should have talked to the administration or written a formal feedback instead of making a comment in the heat of the moment. That way, my concerns would have been addressed in a more appropriate manner, and I wouldn't have risked coming off as the asshole. In the end, I think it's important to balance expressing my feelings with maintaining respect and professionalism, even towards someone I don't agree with or who has treated me unfairly. It's not easy, but it's part of growing up and learning how to handle difficult situations maturely.
